meaning: "The Rich One" — Roman lord of the underworld and of buried wealth

pronunciation.note: Latin Plūtō carries two long vowels, both marked by the restoration. His name is Rome's calque of the Greek Πλούτων — "the Rich One" — the underworld god whose buried wealth made death and riches share a single name. Both vowels are long in the classical scansion; Lewis & Short print the macrons that the restoration keeps.

domains.title: The Rich One Below
domains.subtitle: Underworld, Wealth, and the Doors of the Deep
domains.lead: Plūtō is Rome's underworld god in his own right — not merely Hádēs renamed, but the Latin "Rich One" who rules the dead and the buried treasure together: the god in whose name the ground gives up both its wealth and its silence.

cards.name: The Doors
cards.desc: The Plutonia — the underworld gates; Rome's own door to his realm stood at the Tarentum in the Campus Martius, opened three days a year.

cards.name: Plūtus
cards.desc: His twin-name: the wealth-god Plutus — cornucopia from below, Demeter's son in the Greek telling.

cards.name: Cerberus
cards.desc: The three-headed hound of the threshold — the deep's own border guard, charmed once by Orpheus' song.

cards.name: Proserpina
cards.desc: The queen he took by force and kept by season — Rome's Persephonē, arbiter of the returning year.

symbols.name: The bident
symbols.meaning: His two-pronged staff — the scepter of the depths

symbols.name: The cornucopia
symbols.meaning: Wealth rising from the earth — his benign face as Plūtus

symbols.name: The cypress
symbols.meaning: The underworld's tree — the dark column of the graveyard

symbols.name: Cerberus
symbols.meaning: The three-headed threshold-guard who admits the dead and refuses the living

symbols.name: The narcissus
symbols.meaning: The flower that sprang as a trap in the meadow and lured Proserpina within reach of the deep (Ovid, Met. 5.392–401)

symbols.name: The pomegranate
symbols.meaning: The seed that binds the queen to her season — six seeds, six months below

mythology.lead: Plūtō's Roman myths retell the Greek cycle with a merchant's accent: the underworld as treasury as much as tribunal. Ovid gives the rape of Proserpina, Virgil and Ovid the one descent that moved him, Apollodorus the thieves who failed, Hesiod the older wealth-god beneath the name, and Rome's own calendars the gate that opened three days a year.

myths.title: Proserpina in the Meadow
myths.text: Ovid tells the Roman rape with a landscape's grief (Metamorphoses 5.385–571). In the meadow below Henna, Proserpina gathers flowers — violets, lilies, crocuses — and laughs when the narcissus springs up, a trap set by Venus for the sake of her son Cupid's empire. The ground opens; Plūtō, 'the lord of the dark', carries her down through the pool of Cyane, whose waters, forbidden to speak, dissolve the nymph herself into a spring. Cerēs searches with torches lit at Etna's flame; she turns the mocking boy Ascalabus into a spotted gecko, and opens the cattle of the old man who sheltered her until he curses his own gift. Jupiter arbitrates: the girl who has eaten is bound to the deep. Six pomegranate seeds — or one, in the older Greek telling — divide the year between mother and husband, spring and summer above, autumn and winter below. The myth is Rome's charter for the agricultural year: what is buried is not lost, and what returns must first have descended.

myths.title: Orpheus Charms the Deep
myths.text: When Orpheus lost Eurydice to a snake, he did what no mortal does: he went down singing. Virgil's account (Georgics 4.453–527) makes the underworld itself soften — the Danaids' urn rests, Ixion's wheel stands still, Tityos' vultures pause — and Ovid adds (Metamorphoses 10.1–85) that even the king and queen of the deep wept, a first for both. The condition was set: lead her up, and do not look back until you stand in daylight. At the very border, love or doubt turned his head, and she was reclaimed — a second death, and this one his own doing. The Romans read the myth as Plūtō's one audited exception: the deep can be moved, exactly once, and only by the thing it does not possess — a mortal voice persuasive enough to make law pause. Every later descent of European poetry, Dante's, Monteverdi's, Gluck's, walks the same road under the same rule.

myths.title: Theseus and Pirithous on the Throne of Forgetfulness
myths.text: Not all who descended came to sing. Pirithous, having rashly sworn to marry a daughter of the highest god, persuaded his friend Theseus to descend with him and carry off Proserpina herself (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.12; Epitome 1.24). They sat upon the Chair of Forgetfulness and could not rise, their limbs bound by serpents, until Heracles — come below on his own errand for the hound — wrenched Theseus free and left Pirithous fixed in the stone of the deep, where some say he remains. The failed abduction is the myth's own footnote to the wisdom of Solon, who warned Croesus that no man may count himself happy before the end. The moral Plūtō keeps is plain and grammatical rather than cruel: the dead belong below, the living above, and the queen between is not a prize but a treaty. The exceptions are famous precisely because they are singular — one singer admitted, two thieves impaled, and the border back in order by morning.

myths.title: Plūtus the Giver
myths.text: His older Greek identity is Ploutos, Wealth — born to Demeter and the mortal Iasion 'in the thrice-ploughed fallow' (Hesiod, Theogony 969–974), and granted by Demeter to bless 'all mortal men' in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (486–489). The folk logic is geological: wealth — grain, ore, treasure — comes from under the earth, and so the lord of under the earth is its giver. Aristophanes' comedy Plutus made him a blind old steward whose healed sight showers the just with gold — a fantasy Athens understood as precisely that. Rome kept the word's double truth: as Plūtō he is the treasury, as Dis the grave, and the same soil feeds both accounts. No ancient ever mistook him for safe; but properly approached he was the most reliable of gods — the only one whose gifts were audited every harvest and whose invoices were paid in seed corn.

myths.title: The Mundus and the Secular Games
myths.text: Rome's own door to his kingdom stood at the Tarentum in the Campus Martius, a roofed pit — the mundus — opened by the pontiffs only three days a year, when, as Festus and Servius (ad Aen. 3.104) report, 'the door of the gloomy god is open' and no public business is done. Its greatest rite came in the republic's darkest hour: in 249 BCE the Sibylline books ordered the first Ludi Saeculares, sacrifices and games to Dis Pater and Proserpina to turn the First Punic War (Valerius Maximus 2.4.5; Zosimus 2.1–3). Augustus revived the games in 17 BCE with a liturgy preserved on stone (CIL VI 32323): after the daylight offerings to the Fates, the Ilithyiae, and Earth Mother, the city sacrificed at night, on the Tarentum, to Dis and Proserpina. The gate-myth is the state cult in miniature — Rome does not live with its underworld; it schedules it, opens it three days a year, and closes the door before the business of living resumes.

lore.syncretism: His equation with the Greek Hádēs was total and early, but Rome kept the distinction of names: Hádēs the Unseen, Plūtō the Rich — the wealth-emphasis distinctly Roman. Etruria's Aita presides over his infernal quarter of the Piacenza bronze liver, beside Phersipnai; Gaul's Dis Pater, whom Caesar (Bellum Gallicum 6.18) reports as the ancestor the Gauls claimed, absorbed the cult northward. The mystery religions deepened the syncretism: in the Orphic-Platonic tradition Plouton rules the generative womb of the earth, whence seeds rise, and the Orphic Hymn to Plouton invokes him as 'wealth-giver' and earth-shaker. Late antique Hermetists and the medieval alchemists kept 'plutonic' for all deep-earth fire — the lineage that ends in the element plutonium, named in 1941 for the planet that had taken the god's name. The Romans worshipped the giver and walled out the taker, and quietly knew them for one door.
lore.culturalLegacy: The dwarf planet, discovered in 1930 and named at the suggestion of the eleven-year-old Venetia Burney, carries his name — and the irony is his: the richest name in the sky given to the smallest body, demoted in 2006 and beloved still. Walt Disney's Pluto debuted the same year, a dog answering to the god of the underworld; Glenn T. Seaborg's plutonium (1941) took the name secondhand from the planet. 'Plutocracy' is his grammar of wealth, 'plutonic' his geology of deep-formed stone; financiers still speak of markets' 'underworld' without knowing they are citing him. In the Renaissance his image became Fortune's dark twin — cornucopia in one hand, bident in the other — and every treasury and cemetery remains his bookkeeping. He asked only one question of the living: what will you trust to the deep, and what will it give back in your season?
lore.extendedMeditation:
Plūtō is the god of what the ground holds: the dead, the ore, the seed, the secret. Rome's insight was to give all four one name and one address — the rich dark below where everything valuable also fears to go. He asks the miner's and the mourner's common question: what will you trust to the deep — and what, in your season, will it give back?

The poets gave him two names because one was not enough: the Rich One for the harvesters, the Unseen for everyone else. Rome's honesty was to worship the first and schedule the second — the mundus opened three days a year, the Tarentum lit at night — and to know they were the same door. The deep gives; the deep keeps; the deep does not explain.

The Secular Games at his gate are Rome's darkest and most instructive festival: when the city could not win, it gave the powers below three nights of sacrifice and theater, and history says the war turned. Plūtō's lesson is the one empires learn last — the deep takes payment in advance, in courage, and returns it as history. Every treasury and every cemetery is his bookkeeping, and he never once missed an entry.

lore.archaeology: His monuments are pits and absences. In 1888 workmen on the Quirinal uncovered a subterranean altar-chamber identified with the Tarentum, the roofed pit where Rome sacrificed to Dis Pater and Proserpina — the closest archaeology comes to his door. The Severan copy of the Augustan acta (CIL VI 32323) preserves the 17 BCE liturgy in stone, including the nocturnal offerings to the 'inferis' on three successive nights. Before Rome, Etruria painted his face: the tombs of Tarquinia — the Tomb of the Augurs, the Tomb of the Leopards — banquet amid underworld watch-dogs and demons two centuries before the Secular Games, and funerary urns from Chiusi show Aita wrenching Phersipnai into his chariot. Rome's own grand Plūtō-temple is a negative space the texts acknowledge: the city preferred to worship the giver with Cerēs and to wall the taker into three dark days.
